The growth has been largely catalyzed by Jupiter, the largest trading platform on Solana, which has processed over 80 million trades this month, up +38% month-over-month.

To put this into perspective, Solana has now seen +185% growth in weekly spot DEX trade volumes compared to the lows seen in July.

Crypto markets are on fire.

Bitcoin is pumping, but US spot demand still isn’t confirming the move.

The Coinbase Premium is back below 0, meaning BTC trades slightly cheaper on Coinbase than on Binance.

That doesn’t guarantee a retrace, but without stronger spot buying, the rally could be easier for perp traders to fade.

IMO, 3 things need to happen:

1. The Coinbase Premium needs to reclaim zero.
2. It needs to remain positive, not just briefly cross above it.
3. Ideally, it should rise alongside BTC, showing that Coinbase buyers are supporting the move.

The rally can continue without this, but a sustained positive premium would make it much more convincing.

For now, I’m watching to see whether US spot demand catches up with the price.

U.S. diesel hit $6.529 a gallon, up 24.4 cents in a single week and up $2.78, or 74%, from a year ago.

Nearly every good you buy was ultimately delivered to its end point by truck, and trucks move roughly 72% of U.S. freight by weight, so a diesel spike becomes a cost increase embedded in everything on the shelf. 

The pass-through is fast because most carrier fuel surcharges are indexed directly to this exact EIA weekly average. When this number moves, freight invoices reset within days, and those costs flow into wholesale prices and then onto retail shelves over the following weeks.

The Midwest jumped 43 cents in one week to $6.68 a gallon, and that is important because it is where grain, fertilizer, and farm equipment move. Food input costs will feel this well before the CPI report shows it.

Companies now have two choices: raise prices or absorb the hit to margins. Either way someone pays, and the Fed is staring at a goods inflation impulse that rate policy cannot fix.

thread_tweets.text:
My approach was to evaluate each data center with satellite imagery, look at filings and identify the loudest equipment (typically cooling towers or gas turbines), find the nearest cluster of 5+ homes, and measure that distance. 

From those distances and assumptions about the equipment and the terrain, I was able to derive a modeled noise estimate in dBA. I compared this against a history of verified complaints for each data center.

thread_tweets.text:
The main thing that shocked me was how close some of these absolutely enormous facilities are to neighborhoods.

11 of the 25 are less than 500 meters from a residential cluster. The closest is about 90 meters.

Contrary to what I thought, these are not all remote campuses in the middle of nowhere. Some are practically in people’s backyards.

Proximity isn’t destiny.

For 17 of the 25, I found no credible current operating noise complaint. 

Four had limited allegations or substantially remediated issues. Four had more substantial documented concerns.

The problems concentrate among the larger campuses closest to homes.

It's very easy to predict based on two variables (size in MW and distance from residential clusters) whether a data center will create complaints.

Contrary to what I thought, these are not all remote campuses in the middle of nowhere. Some are practically in people’s backyards.

Proximity isn’t destiny.

For 17 of the 25, I found no credible current operating noise complaint. 

Four had limited allegations or substantially remediated issues. Four had more substantial documented concerns.

The problems concentrate among the larger campuses closest to homes.

It's very easy to predict based on two variables (size in MW and distance from residential clusters) whether a data center will create complaints.

SpaceXAI's Colossus 2 in Mississippi was the worst case in the sample. It's also the biggest data center in America. 

An enormous campus, a large fleet of onsite gas turbines, and a residential cluster roughly 400 meters from the turbine source. Another group of homes is closer still to cooling equipment.

Resident complaints are extensively corroborated. This isn't generic anti-AI sentiment.

Compare that with AWS New Carlisle. 

It has 910 MW of  powered IT capacity, with the nearest qualifying residential cluster about 540 meters from the selected noise source.

I didn’t identify an ongoing operating-noise dispute there. It has other controversies, but noise doesn’t seem to be one of them.

Big and close does not automatically mean bad neighbor.

Equipment matters too. A campus running gas turbines routinely is a different proposition from one with generators sitting idle for emergencies.

Cooling fans can also be a serious nuisance, but in general, turbines are worse. This is going to be a bigger problem going forward because more data centers are going "behind the meter" and building their own generation.  

I modeled approximate sound levels at the homes using equipment assumptions, distance, and shielding. These are estimates, not measurements. Someone (who is not me) should do an acoustic study. No one has done one.

The simplest finding is the most intuitive: distance helps enormously.

Every site with a concern score of 3 or above (higher = noisier) was within 500 meters of a residential cluster. Every site at 800 meters or more scored 1.

That’s not a universal “800 meters is safe” rule. But residential separation is an easy place to start.

The encouraging part is that mitigation can work.

At Microsoft’s Mount Pleasant campus, the company found that cooling fans were creating a tonal noise and changed their operation. This substantially resolved the problem. 

Setbacks, equipment selection, silencers, barriers, and operating changes matter. “There’s a data center nearby” does not have to mean “you can’t sleep.”

My takeaway isn’t “data centers are harmless,” and it certainly isn’t “stop building them.” Noise is a real problem at some of the largest data centers in the US. 

Supporting the AI buildout doesn’t require dismissing its nearest neighbors. It will be much easier to defend if they can sleep through it.

People said radiologists would be gone, in fact, they’re more in demand than ever. They said “half of entry-level jobs will be gone in 9 months”, which was wrong. So the 10% extinction number was just as credible “it’s entirely made up”.

Nvidia has effectively become the central bank of the AI buildout.

Earnings move up the stack over time, toward the application layer. That is where you overearn for longest.

Jensen was the most coherent I have heard anyone on research versus engineering. I was trained as an electrical engineer. We are all freaking out about research, but translation is the hard part, and I view translating research into engineering almost as biology. Look at the probability of success on any biological drug. That is a lab result someone is trying to turn into a working product, and it lands in the low to mid single digits. Even with the smartest people attacking it. 

Things that are magical in research often never make it out.

4. Gwynne and Elon: Gwynne: audacity is a feature. Not the best you can find, the best. Audacity attracts them, then you let them run. I have been thinking about it in my own businesses. How many times do I find the best I can get and then allocate them to something incremental?

Elon came on after a morning of people saying P(doom) was overblown and said the risk is very real. He is in the middle of a Grok training run, so he sees things. The person I trust most on this is Elon, then Jensen and Demis. Twenty years in public and you know every aspect of a person. The people running the frontier shops have been in the spotlight for a fraction of that, and we are still learning how they process information.

I asked him what "Dario is right" meant. The harm, not the regulatory fix. His peer-review proposal is brilliant and de-escalates the moment. It separates the engineering organizations from the research ones and shows who is exaggerating.

It also fixes evals, which are massively overfit. Best line on X: "your girlfriend's a 10 but she's a benchmark maxer."

Eight heterogeneous testers and the overfitting goes away. None of it works without the audit log. 

The next harness is organizational: intention, governance, verification, evidence. Those words sounded boring until this week.

5. Meta and Louisiana: Data centers poll minus 80 nationally, but local polls where data centers are actually built point the other way. How can this gap exist?

My question on stage was why this misinformation campaign is winning so soundly in America. My own answer: a lot of people do not want this group to succeed, for political or organizational reasons, so they glom onto anything. As often as you debunk one, a new one pops up.

You will hear "RSI" over and over for the next 18 months. Put any app in a recursive self-improvement loop with time as the reward function and Microsoft Word will keep you there for nine hours.

6. Naveen Rao: We got a glimpse of what the future of chips could look like. Naveen’s premise is that your brain runs no linear algebra and no floating-point math. The physics of the neurons is what produces the intelligence. A monkey does it on about one watt, the same as the phone in your pocket.

What that means in plain language is biology is orders of magnitude more efficient at converting energy into intelligence than GPUs. Naveen is trying to re-imagine chips from scratch inspired by nature.

@chamath 7. Between Sessions: In every transformation there are researchers, engineers, and anxious intellectuals. The anxious ones find the long-tail probability and amplify it. They have always existed. Listen to the engineers.

8. Luca Ferrari: What I find exciting about this business is that we’ve seen companies Amgen, Roche, Danaher, Berkshire run this playbook in traditional industries. Nobody had made it work in tech. Now Bending Spoons made it work: a $10,000 first deal, now they’re a $40B company thirteen years later.

The structurally difficult question was always whether you can underwrite these cash flows. Luca is proving they’re underwritable, and you can project them seven, eight, nine years out.

9. Brad Gerstner: On a recent pod we mentioned similarities in the sentiment on AI with the sentiment a few years before the dotcom crisis.Brad took a full session on why the market can keep on going. Tl;dr: earnings, not multiples are carrying the market, and price/earnings numbers are still looking healthy.

“These revenues have never happened before in the history of capitalism,” the collective revenue of the top 3 labs is about $100B. Brad thinks they need to reach ~$180B by end of year to keep the AI trade intact. Why? Well, all hyperscalers are building capacity to rent it. Who’s gonna pay the rent? Frontier AI labs. 

So everyone needs frontier AI labs’s revenue to grow fast enough to amortize the data centers.

10. The Vice President: I asked him why forces inside the United States keep trying to slow us down, even with the President, Jensen, Meta and Microsoft on the same stage. His answer was again going back to the cost to the general population. “You see a backlash when people pay an additional power cost. Now, my response to that is you can't just stop building because of it. What you've got to do is build the things that you need, specifically power.” China has out-generated us in energy since 2005 and now makes three times as much.

“We've just got to build more power and that's how we solve this problem fundamentally.”

@chamath 11. Clavicular: I'm a 2/10 on the looksmaxxing scale.

When you look at the great investors of an asset class, it is usually the case that they have no priors in that asset class. Michael Moritz was a journalist. John Doerr was in Intel chip sales. So there is something to be said for being far away, yeah. But having that curiosity and the ability to network and the ability to think critically about problems.

The Internet Needs Crypto to Survive AI: https://t.co/fmxCTfx146

One of the most exciting, and underrated, developments in crypto atm revolves around this @Bankless conversation with @eastdakota of @Cloudflare.

~20% of all websites are routed through Cloudflare, and in this conversation Matthew tells us that the business model of the Web is under attack. To put it simply, agentic traffic is exploding, and agents don't click on ads, but ads underpin much of the "free" stuff we get online. The infrastructure is creaking under agent load. 

Matthew's assertion is that microtransactions, at a scale not previously seen, will be needed to pay for access to content, as the advertising model of the Web falls apart with agents. Crypto people have talked about microtransactions forever, but it was for people, which never worked, whereas we're now contemplating it for agents.

He says Cloudflare handles ~500M requests per second, and that 1-10% of those requests may be suitable for this microtransaction model. A blockchain environment is the only payment network that could theoretically handle this scale, and it would need to hit 5-50M TPS. 

5-50M TPS in prod dwarfs anything yet attempted in crypto, and is far beyond anything TradFi can handle. There are very few blockchain environments that could conceivably provide this throughput.

Just as important as the scale, is the model and trust assumptions. While Cloudflare may roll this out as a solution for its customers first, what's implicit here is the potential for an entirely new business model for the Web. 

If Cloudflare walks this path, I hope that what they build has permissionless validation, allowing for anyone to audit the network.

Cloudflare has been a torch bearer for the open Internet, and so it only follows that if they're to pioneer a new business model for the Web, that the architecture be an open network. Doing so will engender the most trust, goodwill, and adoption in the long run. 

Web 3.0 is dead, long live Web 3.0.
